q.intro.text: Three granola bars are shared equally by four friends. Everyone gets the same amount, and nothing is left over. How much of a bar does each friend get? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Let's work it out, step by step. Press each step, and watch the picture first.

e.step0.text: Each piece is one fourth of a bar: one bar, shared by four.

e.step1.text: Every friend now has one piece from each of the three bars.

e.step2.text: One friend has three pieces of one fourth. The dashed outline is one whole bar, and the pieces fill three fourths of it.

e.step3.text: Three divided by four is three fourths. The amount that is shared goes on top. The number of friends goes underneath.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why is four the bottom number?

t.intro.text: Now five granola bars are shared by three friends. I'll do the first two steps. Then it's your turn.

t.count.text: Look at one friend's tray. How much of a bar is that?

t.write.text: Now write it as one division. Tap the chips to fill the boxes.

t.whole.text: Is five thirds of a bar more, or less, than one whole bar?

t.done.text: Five thirds is one whole bar and two thirds of another. A share can be more than one.

p.intro.text: Jordan shares two granola bars among five friends, and writes: two divided by five is five halves. Is Jordan right?

p.build.text: Prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. There are fewer bars than friends, so each friend gets less than one bar.

p.c2.text: And five halves is two and a half bars. That's more than all the bars there are, so Jordan's answer can't be right.

p.c3.text: Each bar is cut into five pieces, and each friend takes one piece from each bar: two fifths.

p.done.text: That's a proof. Three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one.
